name: State of Oregon

profile.address: 530, Airport Road Southeast, Salem, Marion County, Oregon, 97301
profile.reading:
The Oregon State Data Center sits at 530 Airport Road Southeast in Salem, the state capital, on a site operated by Enterprise Information Services, the central information technology agency for Oregon's executive branch. The facility functions as consolidated infrastructure hosting under EIS's Data Center Services program, which provides shared data center capacity to state agencies rather than requiring each agency to run its own server rooms. This kind of centralization is a common model among state governments, intended to cut duplicated hardware costs, standardize security practices, and simplify disaster recovery planning across dozens of separate agencies.

Oregon's state government does not publish detailed technical specifications for this facility. There is no public figure for its square footage, its critical IT power draw in megawatts, its cooling architecture, or its redundancy tier. State IT agencies generally treat this kind of operational detail as sensitive, since publishing floor plans, power capacity, or precise security posture for a facility that hosts state government systems, including law enforcement, tax, and health and human services data, could create a security exposure. That gap in the public record is itself informative. It signals that Oregon manages this facility more like critical infrastructure than like a commercial colocation product being marketed for lease.

It is worth being precise about what this facility is not. Salem has drawn a wave of attention in 2026 for a very different, much larger data center proposal from a company called Verrus, a commercial project reported at roughly 5.1 billion dollars in prospective investment, for which Oregon's governor directed the withdrawal of state owned land earlier in the year amid public opposition over water use, electricity demand, and local impact. That Verrus campus is a private commercial venture and has no operational connection to the Oregon State Data Center described here, beyond sharing the same metro area. Confusing the two would materially misrepresent both projects. One is decades old public infrastructure quietly running the state's own computing systems, the other is a large private speculative buildout still working through land and permitting questions.

For now, what the public record establishes about the Oregon State Data Center is limited to its role and its operator. It exists to keep Oregon's own government systems running, it is staffed and managed under Enterprise Information Services, and beyond its street address, its technical footprint has not been made public.

reading:
The State of Oregon runs its own enterprise data centre through the Department of Administrative Services, under Enterprise Information Services and its Data Center Services programme. The building the registry holds is named the Oregon State Data Center and sits at 530 Airport Road Southeast in Salem. Enterprise Information Services gives its own address as 550 Airport Road Southeast, Suite C, Salem 97301, the neighbouring address on the same campus.

Data Center Services describes itself as providing managed IT services, colocation and cloud brokering for agencies within state government and for selected county and city agencies. Its service catalogue describes colocation with multiple power feeds, uninterruptible and filtered power backed by generators, redundant air conditioning, and staffed and automated round the clock monitoring of environment and physical security. It publishes no square footage, no floor plan, no generator count and no megawatt figure of any kind, neither IT load nor the size of the utility service the building draws. Those fields are genuinely absent from the state's own material rather than merely unlocated.

What the state does publish, and what makes this entry substantive, is the price list. A colocation rack is 812.19 dollars a month. An x86 server instance is 22.76 dollars a month, with processor billed at 11.47 dollars per core and memory at 7.83 dollars per gigabyte. Enterprise storage and mainframe storage are each a cent per gigabyte per month, and backup is half a cent. Midrange systems are billed per instance, 5,319.29 dollars a month for an iSeries and 776.59 dollars for a UNIX or Linux instance. Mainframe work is billed by processor minute, 45.99 dollars for batch, 33.65 dollars for DB2 and 159.23 dollars for CICS. Local area network service is 54.84 dollars a month for a twelve port switch, wireless is 17.33 dollars per device, and cloud brokering is charged at 14 percent of the vendor invoice. A state facility that still meters CICS and DB2 by the processor minute and rents iSeries partitions by the month is running a genuine mainframe and midrange estate alongside x86, which is the substantive difference between this building and the commercial operators around it in this registry.

One point of confusion is worth heading off. This state owned facility has no connection to the privately financed Verrus data centre campus proposed near Salem, an approximately 5.1 billion dollar commercial project for which Oregon's governor directed the withdrawal of state owned land in 2026 after public opposition. That is a separate developer, a separate site and a separate proceeding, and the two should never be merged.
